title: The Bell That Must Come Down

nodes.brief: Opening: the reader is a bell-ringer's apprentice of Orisonhold, the monastery-city above the cloud line; the Great Bell Orison has cracked, and the Prioress hands over its bronze Clapper to be carried down thirteen stair-towns to the foundry at Lowgate before the ice-wind season closes the passes in twenty days.

exits.intent: Ask the Prioress what she is not saying

nodes.brief: The reader takes the Clapper straight from the Prioress's hands; describe it (a bronze tongue as long as a forearm, heavy as a child, faintly humming) and the padded cradle, and what it is for (recasting the Great Bell at Lowgate).

exits.intent: Go to pack for the descent

nodes.brief: The reader questions the Prioress; she admits that nobody has come back up from Lowgate in a year, that the Cable Court has been buying the ropeways, and that no bell below has rung true since the master founder left. Include the description of the Clapper (a bronze tongue as long as a forearm, faintly humming) and its purpose.

exits.intent: Go to pack for the descent

nodes.brief: Packing at dawn at the cloister gate; the novices and old ringers see the reader off; the cradle on their back, a water skin, and the ninety steps down ahead.

Arrival in Orisonhold and the Ninety Steps: the cliff-monastery, its bell-towers and mule yards; outfitting, kin and rivals; the reader takes the Clapper and chooses a companion and a rope; the first stairs down. The reader enters with several ways forward.

exits.intent: Ask the way of a stranger

nodes.brief: Mandatory scene at the Mule Yard: the reader decides whether to take Biscuit, a stubborn mule who knows the stairs, or to go alone and light

exits.intent: Take Biscuit the mule to carry the pack
Go down on foot, alone and light

nodes.brief: Mandatory scene at the Rope Store: the reader decides whether to sign for a Guild rope (strong, with the Guild's protection and obligations) or carry their own worn rope

exits.intent: Sign for a Ropewrights' Guild rope

Arrival in The Rope Markets: bazaars slung on cables across the gorge, ropewrights and winch-boys, the Cable Court's toll-houses, a knot-oath, rumours of Lowgate. The reader enters with several ways forward.

exits.intent: Ask the way of a stranger

exits.intent: Take the Cable Court's loan of passage

Ending "The Bell Rings Whole": You give the Clapper to the forge-masters to recast the Great Bell for the lowlands: it arrives unmarked, the knot-oath brings the Ropewrights to hang it, and Orison rings true across the mountain.
Aftermath of "The Bell Rings Whole": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "The Bell Rings Whole": a closing image and a last line for the book.

Ending "A True Bell, No Choir": You give the Clapper to the forge-masters and the bell is recast well, but nobody owes you a favour, and the Ropewrights and the Cable Court both squabble over who may hang it.
Aftermath of "A True Bell, No Choir": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "A True Bell, No Choir": a closing image and a last line for the book.

Ending "The Cracked Note": You give the Clapper to the forge-masters, but the bare bronze is chipped from the climb; the recast bell rings with a flaw in its note that the whole mountain learns to love.
Aftermath of "The Cracked Note": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "The Cracked Note": a closing image and a last line for the book.
Ending "Biscuit Carries It Home": You carry the Clapper back up the mountain to keep it from the furnace; Biscuit shoulders the cradle the whole climb, and Orisonhold gets its bronze back, unrung.
Aftermath of "Biscuit Carries It Home": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "Biscuit Carries It Home": a closing image and a last line for the book.
Ending "The Long Way Up": You carry the Clapper back up the mountain alone, step by step; you reach the cloister changed, with the bronze safe and nobody left who remembers why it mattered.
Aftermath of "The Long Way Up": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "The Long Way Up": a closing image and a last line for the book.
Ending "Ploughshares, No Strings": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades for the Terrace Millers, owing nobody; the terraces are turned and the barley will grow.
Aftermath of "Ploughshares, No Strings": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "Ploughshares, No Strings": a closing image and a last line for the book.
Ending "The Song in the Metal": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades with the Cable Court's debt on your back; the Millers sing the wind-calls into the casting and the blades hum in the furrow.
Aftermath of "The Song in the Metal": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "The Song in the Metal": a closing image and a last line for the book.
Ending "Bronze and Silence": You melt the Clapper into plough-blades with the Cable Court's debt behind you and no wind-calls to speak with the Millers; a quiet, uncertain gift.
Aftermath of "Bronze and Silence": what changes for the people of the mountain and the lowlands, weeks later.
Final page of "Bronze and Silence": a closing image and a last line for the book.
